question:
The following sentence has been divided into four parts. Identify the part that contains an error.
This is / a doll / and there is / a umbrella.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. a umbrella.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the article used before the word "umbrella". Since "umbrella" begins with a vowel sound (the initial "u" here is pronounced as "uh", a vowel sound), it must be preceded by the article "an", not "a".

• Rule — Use of "a" and "an": The article "a" is used before words beginning with a consonant sound, while "an" is used before words beginning with a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u or a silent consonant with a vowel sound).
◦ Example: an umbrella, an hour, an honest man; but a university, a European.

• Applying the rule: "a umbrella" must be corrected to "an umbrella".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "This is" — grammatically correct; a simple demonstrative pronoun with the verb "is".

• Option 2: "a doll" — correct; "doll" begins with a consonant sound, so "a" is the right article.

• Option 3: "and there is" — correct; a correctly formed coordinating clause introducing the next noun.

NOTE

• Words like "hour", "honest", "heir" take "an" because the initial "h" is silent.

• Words like "university", "uniform", "one-eyed", "European" take "a" because they begin with a consonant sound (a "y"/"w" sound), despite starting with a vowel letter.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error mark 'No error' as your answer.
The aeroplane took down / without the passengers after / making a sudden announcement.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The aeroplane took down.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the phrasal verb used. The correct phrasal verb for an aircraft leaving the ground is "took off", not "took down".

• Rule — Phrasal verbs with "take": "Take off" means to leave the ground and begin flying (used for aircraft), while "take down" means to write something down, or to remove/pull down something (e.g. a structure or a poster).
◦ Example: The flight took off an hour late due to fog.

• Applying the rule: "The aeroplane took down" must be corrected to "The aeroplane took off".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "making a sudden announcement" — grammatically correct; a correctly formed present participle phrase.

• Option 2: "No error" — incorrect, since the sentence does contain an error, as explained above.

• Option 3: "without the passengers after" — correct as written; no grammatical fault in this segment.

NOTE

• Other commonly confused phrasal verbs with "take": take off (leave the ground / remove clothing), take down (note down / dismantle), take up (start a hobby/job), take over (assume control), take after (resemble a relative).

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error.
She shall being / travelling / by this time / tomorrow.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. She shall being.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes an action that will be in progress at a specific point of time in the future ("by this time tomorrow"), which requires the Future Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Future Continuous Tense: Subject + shall/will + be + V1+ing. The base form "be" is used after "shall/will", never "being".
◦ Example: She will be travelling by this time tomorrow.

• Applying the rule: "She shall being" must be corrected — the auxiliary must be followed by "be", not "being" (giving "She will be"/"She shall be").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "travelling" — correct; the present participle correctly follows "be" once the auxiliary error is fixed.

• Option 3: "by this time" — correct; a standard time-phrase used with the future continuous tense.

• Option 4: "tomorrow" — correct; correctly indicates the future time reference.

NOTE

• "Shall" is traditionally used with "I" and "we"; "will" is used with all other subjects, though modern usage accepts "will" with all subjects.

• Common Future Continuous time markers: at this time tomorrow, by this time next week, this time next year.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
Emily is a American living in Paris for her work.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. a American.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the article used before the word "American". Since "American" begins with a vowel sound, it must be preceded by the article "an", not "a".

• Rule — Use of "a" and "an": "A" is used before words beginning with a consonant sound; "an" is used before words beginning with a vowel sound.
◦ Example: an American, an artist, an actor.

• Applying the rule: "a American" must be corrected to "an American".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "living in Paris" — correct; a properly formed present participle phrase.

• Option 3: "Emily is" — correct; correct subject-verb agreement (singular subject with "is").

• Option 4: "for her work" — correct; a correctly formed prepositional phrase.

NOTE

• Nationality words beginning with a vowel sound that take "an": an American, an Indian, an Italian, an Australian, an Egyptian.

• Nationality words beginning with a consonant sound that take "a": a British, a Chinese, a French, a German, a Japanese.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The Sun is about 1.4 million kilometres (1)_____diameter, while the Earth is about 13,000 kilometers wide. This indicates that the Sun's width would need to be filled by more than one hundred Earths. Sunspots are dreary (2)_____ on the Sun's surface that are two thousand degrees Celsius cooler than the rest of the surface. The coolest piece of the sunspot is the dim focus called the umbra. The penumbra surrounds it. On the Sun's surface, some sunspots are just specks. Additionally, they appear in groups up to ten times larger than Earth. They can sometimes reach 200,000 miles in length. As the Sun rotates, these groups (3)_____ to travel across the Sun over two weeks. Every 11 years, the number of sunspots reaches its maximum. The solar or sunspot cycle (4)______ to this. The Earth's weather may become more extreme and warm during the peak of sunspot activity. According to the (5)______ made by satellites like Nimbus 7, when sunspots are at their largest, less heat reaches Earth.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. in.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase used to state the measurement of a dimension (diameter, length, width, height) takes the preposition "in", as in "in diameter", "in length", "in width".

• Rule — Prepositions with dimension nouns: When a numerical measurement is followed by a dimension noun like diameter, length, breadth, width or height, the correct preposition to use is "in".
◦ Example: The pipe is two metres in diameter.

• Applying the rule: "about 1.4 million kilometres in diameter" is the grammatically correct phrase.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "of" is incorrect; "of diameter" is not an idiomatic or grammatically accepted phrase for expressing measurement.

• Option 3: "on" is incorrect; "on" indicates position/surface, not measurement.

• Option 4: "at" is incorrect; "at" indicates a point in time or place, not a dimension.

NOTE

• Similar fixed prepositional phrases used with measurements: in length, in breadth, in height, in depth, in weight.

• Compare with age: "He is ten years of age" — here "of" is correct because the noun is "age", not a dimension word like diameter.

According to the (5)______ made by satellites like Nimbus 7, when sunspots are at their largest, less heat reaches Earth.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. regions.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage describes sunspots as darker, cooler areas scattered across the Sun's surface. The most appropriate word to describe such scattered areas is "regions", meaning distinct areas or zones of a surface.

• Rule — Contextual word choice: The chosen word must fit both the grammatical context (a plural countable noun, since "sunspots are dreary ___") and the logical meaning (areas on a surface, not a single continuous strip).

• Applying the rule: "Sunspots are dreary regions on the Sun's surface" correctly conveys that sunspots are patches/areas on the solar surface.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "section" is incorrect; "section" suggests a single defined division, which does not fit the idea of multiple scattered dark spots.

• Option 3: "belt" is incorrect; "belt" implies a long, continuous band (like an asteroid belt), not scattered patches.

• Option 4: "province" is incorrect; "province" refers to an administrative division of a country, contextually irrelevant here.

NOTE

• Words like "regions", "areas", "zones", "patches" are commonly tested in cloze passages describing scattered/localised phenomena.

• Always check both grammatical fit (singular/plural, part of speech) and contextual/logical fit before selecting a cloze answer.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The Sun is about 1.4 million kilometres (1)_____diameter, while the Earth is about 13,000 kilometers wide. This indicates that the Sun's width would need to be filled by more than one hundred Earths. Sunspots are dreary (2)_____ on the Sun's surface that are two thousand degrees Celsius cooler than the rest of the surface. The coolest piece of the sunspot is the dim focus called the umbra. The penumbra surrounds it. On the Sun's surface, some sunspots are just specks. Additionally, they appear in groups up to ten times larger than Earth. They can sometimes reach 200,000 miles in length. As the Sun rotates, these groups (3)_____ to travel across the Sun over two weeks. Every 11 years, the number of sunspots reaches its maximum. The solar or sunspot cycle (4)______ to this. The Earth's weather may become more extreme and warm during the peak of sunspot activity. According to the (5)______ made by satellites like Nimbus 7, when sunspots are at their largest, less heat reaches Earth.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. appear.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes how, from an observer's viewpoint on Earth, the sunspot groups seem to move across the Sun's surface as the Sun rotates. The correct verb to express this sense of "seeming to happen" is "appear".

• Rule — "Appear + to + infinitive": The structure "appear to + V1" means "to seem to do something", commonly used to describe an observed but not necessarily literal phenomenon.
◦ Example: The stars appear to twinkle in the night sky.

• Applying the rule: "these groups appear to travel across the Sun over two weeks" correctly conveys that, as observed, the sunspot groups seem to move across the solar disc due to the Sun's rotation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "act" is incorrect; "act to travel" is not an accepted collocation in English.

• Option 2: "show" is incorrect; "show to travel" is grammatically unacceptable — "show" does not take a "to + infinitive" in this sense.

• Option 3: "shape" is incorrect; "shape" is not used with "to + infinitive" to mean "seem", and it does not fit the context.

NOTE

• Other verbs that take the "to + infinitive" pattern to express perception/seeming: seem to, appear to, tend to, happen to.

• Do not confuse "appear" (to seem / to come into view) with "appeal" (to request or to attract), a common SSC vocabulary trap.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The Sun is about 1.4 million kilometres (1)_____diameter, while the Earth is about 13,000 kilometers wide. This indicates that the Sun's width would need to be filled by more than one hundred Earths. Sunspots are dreary (2)_____ on the Sun's surface that are two thousand degrees Celsius cooler than the rest of the surface. The coolest piece of the sunspot is the dim focus called the umbra. The penumbra surrounds it. On the Sun's surface, some sunspots are just specks. Additionally, they appear in groups up to ten times larger than Earth. They can sometimes reach 200,000 miles in length. As the Sun rotates, these groups (3)_____ to travel across the Sun over two weeks. Every 11 years, the number of sunspots reaches its maximum. The solar or sunspot cycle (4)______ to this. The Earth's weather may become more extreme and warm during the peak of sunspot activity. According to the (5)______ made by satellites like Nimbus 7, when sunspots are at their largest, less heat reaches Earth.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. refers.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence explains that the term "solar or sunspot cycle" is the name given to the 11-year pattern just described. The verb that correctly expresses "to denote/relate to something already mentioned" is "refers".

• Rule — "Refer to": The phrasal verb "refer to" means to mention, indicate, or be related to something. With a third-person singular subject ("the solar or sunspot cycle"), the verb takes the "-s" ending: "refers to".
◦ Example: The term "greenhouse effect" refers to the trapping of heat in the Earth's atmosphere.

• Applying the rule: "The solar or sunspot cycle refers to this" correctly links the named cycle to the 11-year pattern described earlier in the passage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "pass" is incorrect; "pass to this" is not a meaningful or grammatically standard phrase in this context.

• Option 3: "cite" is incorrect; "cite" means to quote or mention as evidence/example, and does not fit grammatically with "to this" in this sense.

• Option 4: "entrust" is incorrect; "entrust" means to assign responsibility or trust to someone, contextually irrelevant here.

NOTE

• Common confusion: "refer to" (to relate/mention) vs. "prefer" (to like more) vs. "defer" (to postpone or yield) — all share the Latin root "ferre" (to carry).

• "Refers to" always needs the preposition "to" when followed by the noun/pronoun it points to.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The Sun is about 1.4 million kilometres (1)_____diameter, while the Earth is about 13,000 kilometers wide. This indicates that the Sun's width would need to be filled by more than one hundred Earths. Sunspots are dreary (2)_____ on the Sun's surface that are two thousand degrees Celsius cooler than the rest of the surface. The coolest piece of the sunspot is the dim focus called the umbra. The penumbra surrounds it. On the Sun's surface, some sunspots are just specks. Additionally, they appear in groups up to ten times larger than Earth. They can sometimes reach 200,000 miles in length. As the Sun rotates, these groups (3)_____ to travel across the Sun over two weeks. Every 11 years, the number of sunspots reaches its maximum. The solar or sunspot cycle (4)______ to this. The Earth's weather may become more extreme and warm during the peak of sunspot activity. According to the (5)______ made by satellites like Nimbus 7, when sunspots are at their largest, less heat reaches Earth.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. observations.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence states that data gathered by satellites like Nimbus 7 shows that less heat reaches Earth when sunspots are largest. The word that correctly describes scientific data gathered by watching/monitoring a phenomenon is "observations".

• Rule — Contextual word choice: The chosen noun must collocate naturally with "made by satellites" and refer to recorded scientific data — "observations" (the recorded results of watching/monitoring something) fits this precisely.
◦ Example: Observations made by weather satellites help scientists track storms.

• Applying the rule: "According to the observations made by satellites like Nimbus 7..." correctly conveys that satellite-recorded data supports the claim about sunspots and Earth's heat.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "perceptions" is incorrect; "perceptions" refers to subjective understanding or interpretation, not objective recorded data from satellites.

• Option 2: "inspections" is incorrect; "inspections" implies a deliberate, close examination (often official), which does not fit the passive, ongoing monitoring done by satellites.

• Option 4: "invalidations" is incorrect; "invalidations" means the act of making something invalid/void, contextually meaningless here.

NOTE

• "Observation" (noting/watching and recording) is frequently confused with "observance" (following a custom, rule, or occasion), a common SSC vocabulary trap.

• Words commonly collocating with "made by": observations made by, decisions made by, discoveries made by, announcements made by.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word segment in the following sentence.
They are leaving there coats there.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. their coats there.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the homophone "there" twice, but it is used incorrectly for the possessive pronoun that should modify "coats". The word required before "coats" is the possessive adjective "their" (belonging to them), while the second "there" (indicating place) is correctly used.

• Rule — There / Their / They're: "There" indicates place/location; "their" is a possessive adjective meaning "belonging to them"; "they're" is the contraction of "they are".
◦ Example: They left their bags there before they're (they are) late.

• Applying the rule: since the coats belong to "them", the correct possessive form is "their coats", while the second "there" (indicating the place where they are leaving the coats) remains unchanged.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "they're coats there" is incorrect; "they're" (they are) cannot function as a possessive adjective before a noun.

• Option 3: "there coats their" is incorrect; it wrongly places "there" before "coats" (should be possessive "their") and wrongly uses "their" at the end (should be the place-word "there").

• Option 4: "their coats their" is incorrect; the second word should indicate place ("there"), not possession ("their") — using "their" twice is wrong.

NOTE

• This is a classic SSC homophone-substitution question. Always identify: does the blank need possession (their), location (there), or a contraction of "they are" (they're)?

• Similarly confused homophone sets often tested: its / it's, your / you're, whose / who's.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the word 'Swap' from the given sentence.
The original buyer attempted to resell the tickets online because there was no option to exchange them for a new date.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. exchange.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Swap" means to exchange one thing for another. (अदला-बदली करना)
◦ Example: The two friends decided to swap their seats for the movie.

• In the given sentence, the word "exchange" carries this exact meaning — replacing the tickets with different ones for a new date — making it the closest synonym of "swap" among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "resell" (फिर से बेचना): means to sell something again, usually to a different buyer — not the same as swapping.

• Option 3: "original" (मूल): means the first or initial one, unrelated in meaning to "swap".

• Option 4: "option" (विकल्प): means a choice available; it does not mean exchange.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "swap": barter, trade, interchange, substitute.

• "Swap" is commonly used informally in spoken English; "exchange" is its more formal equivalent, frequently tested as a synonym pair in SSC exams.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM for the underlined word in the given sentence.
He feels that wealthy people view him with contempt because he is poor.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Admiration.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Contempt" means a feeling that a person or thing is beneath consideration, worthless, or deserving scorn/disrespect. (तिरस्कार / घृणा)
◦ Example: She looked at the cheat with contempt.

• The antonym of "contempt" must express a feeling of high regard or respect, which is exactly what "Admiration" (प्रशंसा) means — a feeling of warm approval or respect for someone.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Derision" (उपहास): means ridicule or mockery — a synonym of contempt, not its antonym.

• Option 3: "Scorn" (तिरस्कार): means open disrespect or contempt — again a synonym, not an antonym.

• Option 4: "Obscurity" (अस्पष्टता / गुमनामी): means the state of being unknown or unclear — unrelated in meaning to "contempt".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "contempt": disdain, disrespect, scorn, derision.

• Other antonyms of "contempt": respect, esteem, regard, reverence.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
She went on a shopping spree with her friend and made him ________ the fat bill.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. pay.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the causative verb "make" in the structure "make + object + base form of verb (V1)", meaning to force/cause someone to do something.

• Rule — Causative "make": Make/Made + Object + V1 (base form, without "to").
◦ Example: The teacher made the students complete their homework.

• Applying the rule: "made him pay the fat bill" correctly uses the base form "pay" after the object "him".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "paid" is incorrect; the past form "paid" cannot follow the causative structure "make + object + V1".

• Option 2: "do" is incorrect; "do" does not collocate with "bill" — one "pays" a bill, one does not "do" a bill.

• Option 4: "give" is incorrect; while it could grammatically follow "made him", "give the fat bill" does not carry the intended meaning of settling a payment — "pay the bill" is the correct collocation.

NOTE

• Causative verbs frequently tested by SSC: make, let, have (all followed by base form V1), and get (followed by "to + V1").
◦ Example: She let him go. / She got him to go. / She had him clean the room.

question:
Identify the incorrectly spelt word and select its correct spelling.
You shall recieve proper pay for your work.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. receive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "receive" — meaning to be given, presented with, or paid something.
◦ Example: Employees receive their salary on the last working day of the month.

• Spelling key: remember the rule "i before e, except after c". Since the word contains the letter "c" just before this vowel combination, the correct order is "ei", giving "rec-EI-ve", not "rec-IE-ve".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "resieve" — incorrect; this is merely another incorrect spelling of the same word ("receive"), with both the "s" (should be "c") and the vowel order ("ie" instead of "ei") wrong.

• Option 2: "propper" — incorrect; this is a wrong spelling of a different word, "proper" (which has only one "p" in the middle), and does not correct the misspelled word "recieve" in the sentence.

• Option 4: "propeer" — incorrect; likewise a wrong spelling of "proper", not a correction of "recieve".

NOTE

• The "i before e, except after c" rule applies to words like: believe, achieve, chief, receive, deceive, ceiling.

• Common exceptions to this rule: weird, seize, either, neither, science.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Transient
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Permanent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Transient" means lasting for only a short time; temporary or fleeting. (क्षणिक / अस्थायी)
◦ Example: Fame in showbiz can often be transient.

• The antonym must mean "lasting" or "enduring", which is exactly what "Permanent" (स्थायी) means — lasting or intended to last indefinitely.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Transparent" (पारदर्शी): means clear or easy to see through — unrelated in meaning to "transient".

• Option 3: "Transitory" (क्षणभंगुर): is a synonym of "transient" (also means short-lived), not its antonym.

• Option 4: "Irregular" (अनियमित): means not following a regular pattern — unrelated to the idea of duration.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "transient": temporary, fleeting, momentary, ephemeral.

• Other antonyms of "transient": permanent, lasting, enduring, everlasting.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Innocent
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Guilty.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Innocent" means not guilty of a crime or offence; free from moral wrong. (निर्दोष)
◦ Example: The court found the accused innocent of all charges.

• The antonym must mean "responsible for wrongdoing", which is exactly what "Guilty" (दोषी) means — having committed an offence or wrong.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Mischievous" (शरारती): means playfully naughty or causing minor trouble — not the direct opposite of "innocent" in the legal/moral sense intended here.

• Option 3: "Unfair" (अनुचित): means not just or equitable — unrelated to guilt or innocence.

• Option 4: "Righteous" (धर्मी): means morally right or virtuous — actually closer in meaning to "innocent" than opposite to it.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "innocent": blameless, guiltless, naive, pure.

• Other antonyms of "innocent": guilty, culpable, corrupt, sinful.

question:
Select the correct spelling of the underlined word.
He is one of the most underated players in the team.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Underrated.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Underrated" — meaning rated or valued below one's true worth.
◦ Example: She is an underrated singer who deserves far more recognition.

• Spelling key: the word is formed from the prefix "under-" + the verb "rate" + the suffix "-d", giving under + rated = underrated — a double "r" (from "under" + "rated"), and a single "t".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Undereted" — incorrect; it drops the letter "r" from "rate" entirely, distorting the root word.

• Option 2: "Underatted" — incorrect; it wrongly doubles the "t" instead of the "r", and drops one "r" from "under".

• Option 4: "Underreted" — incorrect; it misspells "rated" as "reted", changing the vowel sound of the root word.

NOTE

• Similarly formed words with the prefix "under-": underrate, underestimate, undermine, underperform, undergo.

• Related word: "overrated" (valued above true worth) — the direct antonym of "underrated".

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
To be at daggers drawn
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Ready to fight.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To be at daggers drawn" means to be in a state of intense hostility or open enmity with someone, ready to fight or quarrel. (आपस में कट्टर दुश्मनी होना)
◦ Example: The two business partners have been at daggers drawn ever since the disputed merger.

• The idiom originates from the image of two people literally drawing daggers (knives) against each other, symbolising extreme hostility and readiness for confrontation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "To be about to collapse" — describes physical weakness or imminent failure, unrelated to hostility between people.

• Option 3: "Under suspicion" — means being doubted or distrusted, different from open hostility/readiness to fight.

• Option 4: "To be under control" — means being managed or restrained, essentially the opposite of the aggressive, uncontrolled hostility implied by the idiom.

NOTE

• Other idioms expressing hostility/conflict often asked in SSC: "To be at loggerheads" (in strong disagreement), "To cross swords with someone" (to argue/fight with someone), "To be up in arms" (to be very angry and ready to protest).

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The hotel room, / which we / booked, / isn't enough big.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. isn't enough big.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the word order of "enough" with an adjective. When "enough" modifies an adjective, it must be placed AFTER the adjective, not before it.

• Rule — Position of "enough": Adjective + enough (e.g., big enough, good enough, old enough); but enough + noun (e.g., enough time, enough money).
◦ Example: The room isn't big enough for a king-size bed.

• Applying the rule: "isn't enough big" must be corrected to "isn't big enough".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "The hotel room," — correct; a properly formed subject noun phrase.

• Option 3: "which we" — correct; a properly formed relative clause introduction.

• Option 4: "booked," — correct; correctly completes the relative clause "which we booked".

NOTE

• "Enough" as an adjective-modifier always follows the adjective: tall enough, strong enough, fast enough.

• "Enough" as a noun-modifier always precedes the noun: enough water, enough chairs, enough patience.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Appalled
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Disgusted.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Appalled" means filled with horror, shock, or strong dismay/disgust at something bad or wrong. (स्तब्ध / घृणा से भरा हुआ)
◦ Example: She was appalled by the poor condition of the hospital.

• Among the given options, "Disgusted" (घृणित) — feeling strong revulsion or disapproval — comes closest to the shocked, horrified reaction conveyed by "appalled".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Applied" (लागू किया गया): means put into practical use — unrelated in meaning to "appalled".

• Option 2: "Clap" (ताली बजाना): means to strike the palms together to applaud — unrelated in meaning to "appalled".

• Option 4: "Allied" (संबद्ध): means joined or united for a common purpose — unrelated to "appalled".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "appalled": horrified, shocked, dismayed, aghast.

• Do not confuse "appalled" (shocked/disgusted) with "applauded" (praised by clapping) — a common sound-alike trap in SSC vocabulary questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Cramped
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Spacious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Cramped" means (of a space) too small; lacking sufficient room to move or fit comfortably. (तंग / भीड़भाड़ वाला)
◦ Example: The five of them were cramped into a tiny two-seater car.

• The antonym must mean "having ample room", which is exactly what "Spacious" (विशाल / खुला) means — having a lot of space.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Filthy" (गंदा): means extremely dirty — unrelated to the idea of space.

• Option 3: "Tight" (तंग): means fitting closely, with little room — a synonym of "cramped", not its antonym.

• Option 4: "Crammed" (ठूंसा हुआ): means packed tightly full — a synonym of "cramped", not its antonym.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "cramped": confined, packed, congested, crowded.

• Other antonyms of "cramped": spacious, roomy, ample, open.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
Even in cold weather, the reliable car always started on the first try.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. dependable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Reliable" means able to be trusted to do what is expected; consistently good in quality or performance. (भरोसेमंद)
◦ Example: He is a reliable friend who always keeps his word.

• Among the given options, "Dependable" (विश्वसनीय) — able to be relied or counted upon — is the closest synonym, matching the sense that the car could always be trusted to start.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "inaccurate" (गलत): means not correct or precise — an unrelated sense.

• Option 3: "erratic" (अनियमित): means unpredictable or inconsistent — essentially the opposite of "reliable".

• Option 4: "flaky" (अस्थिर स्वभाव का): (informal) means unreliable or prone to unpredictable behaviour — again roughly opposite in meaning to "reliable".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "reliable": trustworthy, dependable, consistent, steady.

• Other antonyms of "reliable": unreliable, erratic, unpredictable, undependable.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
To cost an arm and a leg
option_3: Someone does not have money to buy something
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Something is very expensive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To cost an arm and a leg" means to be extremely/exorbitantly expensive. (बहुत महंगा होना)
◦ Example: That designer handbag cost her an arm and a leg.

• The idiom likely originates from the idea that something is so valuable/costly that paying for it would be as painful or as great a sacrifice as losing a limb.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Someone is badly hurt" — describes a literal physical injury, not the figurative meaning of the idiom.

• Option 3: "Someone does not have money to buy something" — describes a lack of funds, related to but not the actual meaning of the idiom (the idiom describes the high price, not the buyer's poverty).

• Option 4: "Someone has borne losses" — refers to suffering a financial loss, different from the meaning "very expensive".

NOTE

• Other idioms about expense/money often asked in SSC: "To pay through the nose" (to pay an excessively high price), "A steal" (something bought very cheaply), "To break the bank" (to cost more than one can afford).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
The news gave him inexpressible ecstasy.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Depression.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Ecstasy" means an overwhelming feeling of great happiness or joyful excitement. (परमानंद / अत्यधिक हर्ष)
◦ Example: The fans were in a state of ecstasy when their team won the championship.

• The antonym must express an extreme feeling of sadness or low spirit, which is exactly what "Depression" (अवसाद / निराशा) means — a state of severe despondency and dejection.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Delight" (आनंद): means great pleasure — a synonym of "ecstasy" (though milder in degree), not its antonym.

• Option 2: "Passion" (जुनून): means strong emotion or enthusiasm — not opposite in meaning to "ecstasy".

• Option 4: "Disappointment" (निराशा): means mild sadness at unmet expectations — a much weaker feeling than the extreme opposite required to counter "ecstasy"; "depression" better captures the intensity of the opposite emotional extreme.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "ecstasy": elation, euphoria, rapture, bliss.

• Other antonyms of "ecstasy": depression, misery, despair, gloom.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Mrs. Lakshmi's purchases add around to ₹2,650.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. purchases add up to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb required here is "add up to", which means to total or amount to a certain figure.

• Rule — Phrasal verb "add up to": Add up to is used when stating the sum total of a set of quantities/amounts. The fixed preposition combination is "up to", not "around to", "out to", "from to", or "for to".
◦ Example: All her expenses add up to ₹5,000 this month.

• Applying the rule: "Mrs. Lakshmi's purchases add up to ₹2,650" correctly conveys that her purchases total this amount.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "purchases add out to" is incorrect; "add out to" is not a recognised phrasal verb in English.

• Option 2: "purchases add from to" is incorrect; "add from to" is not a grammatically valid phrase.

• Option 4: "purchases add for to" is incorrect; "add for to" is not a recognised phrasal verb or valid construction.

NOTE

• Other useful phrasal verbs with "add": add up (to make sense / to calculate a total), add on (to include something extra), add in (to include as part of something).

• Do not confuse "add up to" (to total) with "amount to" (also means to total, a close synonym).
